pg_21__page_1_Figure_2.jpeg.description: A horizontal number line marked with tick marks labeled with integers from -5 to 5, spaced at equal intervals. An arrow at the right end indicates the direction of increasing values.

pg_21__page_4_Picture_1.jpeg.description: A line drawing of a scientific calculator, featuring an LCD display at the top, two rows of smaller function buttons, and a grid of keypad buttons below.

pg_21__page_9_Diagram_29.jpeg.description: A geometric diagram illustrating the expansion of the product of two binomials, (a + b)(c + d), using the area of a rectangle divided into four smaller regions. The overall rectangle has a total height of a + b (split vertically into top section 'a' and bottom section 'b') and a total width of c + d (split horizontally into left section 'c' and right section 'd'). Dashed lines divide the main rectangle into four sub-rectangles with labeled areas: top-left area is ac, top-right area is ad, bottom-left area is bc, and bottom-right area is bd. Dimension arrows indicate lengths a, b, c, d, c + d along the sides, and a + b along the right side.

pg_21__page_23_Figure_15.jpeg.description: A number line oriented from left to right showing four labeled tick marks: b + c, b, a + c, and a, in that order from left to right. This illustrates the effect of adding a negative value c to both a and b, shifting both points to the left while preserving their relative order (b < a and b + c < a + c).

pg_21__page_24_Figure_13.jpeg.description:
A sign diagram representing the signs of factors and their product across a real number line marked with -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4.

Vertical reference lines are drawn downwards at x = 1 and x = 3.

1. First row, for x - 1:
- Dashed line (negative) for x < 1.
- Open circle at x = 1.
- Solid line (positive) for x > 1.

2. Second row, for 3 - x:
- Solid line (positive) for x < 3.
- Open circle at x = 3.
- Dashed line (negative) for x > 3.

3. Third row, for the product (x - 1)(3 - x):
- Dashed line (negative) for x < 1.
- Open circle at x = 1.
- Solid line (positive) between x = 1 and x = 3.
- Open circle at x = 3.
- Dashed line (negative) for x > 3.

pg_21__page_25_Figure_9.jpeg.description:
A sign diagram representing the sign variation of linear factors and a rational expression across intervals on a number line with key boundary points at -1, 0, 1, 2, and 3.

Left vertical labels and corresponding horizontal lines:
- Expression p: Has an open circle at x = 0. It is dashed to the left (negative) and solid to the right (positive).
- Expression p - 2: Has an open circle at x = 2. It is dashed to the left (p < 2) and solid to the right (p > 2).
- Expression p - 1: Has an open circle at x = 1. It is dashed to the left (p < 1) and solid to the right (p > 1).
- Combined rational expression p(p - 2)/(p - 1): Has open circles at x = 0 and x = 2 (where the expression equals 0), an asterisk/cross at x = 1 (where it is undefined), dashed lines indicating negative intervals (p < 0 and 1 < p < 2), and solid lines indicating positive intervals (0 < p < 1 and p > 2).

pg_21__page_26_Figure_4.jpeg.description:
An incorrect sign diagram illustrating common errors when analyzing algebraic expressions. The diagram features a number line at the top with labeled points at -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, and 2, with vertical grid lines extending down from -3, -1, and 2.

On the left, four expressions are listed horizontally:
1. x - 2: Represented by a dashed line to the left of x = 2 and a solid line to the right, with an open circle at x = 2.
2. 3(x + 1): Represented by a dashed line to the left of x = -1 and a solid line to the right, with an open circle at x = -1.
3. x + 3: Represented by a dashed line to the left of x = -3 and a solid line to the right, with an open circle at x = -3.
4. ((x - 2) + 3(x + 1)) / (x + 3): Represented by a dashed line to the left of x = -3, a star at x = -3, a solid line between -3 and -1, an open circle at x = -1, a dashed line between -1 and 2, an open circle at x = 2, and a solid line to the right of 2.

A large curly bracket encompasses all four rows on the right, labeled with the word "Wrong!" to indicate that combining signs in this manner for addition in the numerator is mathematically incorrect.

pg_21__page_28_Figure_11.jpeg.description:
A number line labeled with integer points from -5 to 7 displaying three intervals:
1. Interval A: A blue line segment from -4 to -2, with solid dots (included endpoints) at both -4 and -2, representing the closed interval [-4, -2].
2. Interval B: A blue line segment starting at 0 with a solid dot and extending to 1 with an arrowhead pointing right, representing the half-open interval [0, 1).
3. Interval C: A blue line segment extending from 2 to 5 with arrowheads at both ends (pointing left at 2 and right at 5), representing the open interval (2, 5).

pg_21__page_30_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
A horizontal number line marked from -7 to 7 with tick marks at integer intervals. Above the number line, two distances are illustrated with double-headed horizontal arrows:
1. A segment spanning between -5 and -3, labeled above with the equation "|-3 - (-5)| = 2".
2. A segment spanning between 2 and 7, labeled above with the equation "|7 - 2| = 5".

pg_21__page_71_Diagram_3.jpeg.description:
Four Venn diagrams labeled from left to right illustrating set operations:
1. Subset ($C \subseteq A$): A large circle labeled $A$ entirely contains a smaller inner circle labeled $C$.
2. Union ($A \cup B$): Two overlapping circles labeled $A$ and $B$, with both circles entirely shaded light blue.
3. Intersection ($A \cap B$): Two overlapping circles labeled $A$ and $B$, with only the overlapping region between them shaded light blue.
4. Difference ($A \setminus B$): Two overlapping circles labeled $A$ and $B$, with only the portion of circle $A$ that does not overlap with circle $B$ shaded light blue.

pg_21__page_71_Diagram_8.jpeg.description: A Venn diagram showing three overlapping circles labeled A, B, and C. Circle A is on the top-left, Circle B is on the top-right, and Circle C is at the bottom. The shaded area consists of the intersection of A and B, plus the intersection of A and C, covering the region (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C).

pg_21__page_71_Diagram_10.jpeg.description:
A Venn diagram showing three intersecting sets labeled A (top-left circle), B (top-right circle), and C (bottom circle). The regions are numbered (1) through (8):
- (1): The region in A and B, but not C.
- (2): The region in B and C, but not A.
- (3): The region in A and C, but not B.
- (4): The region exclusively in A.
- (5): The region exclusively in B.
- (6): The region exclusively in C.
- (7): The central intersection region belonging to all three sets A, B, and C.
- (8): The region outside all three circles A, B, and C.

Regions (1), (3), and (7) are shaded light blue, representing the set expression (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C), which is the region where set A intersects with either B or C.

pg_21__page_79_Figure_2.jpeg.description: A line graph showing the Laffer curve, which plots Tax Revenue on the vertical axis against Tax Rate on the horizontal axis. The curve starts at the origin (0% tax rate, 0 tax revenue), rises smoothly as the tax rate increases until it reaches a maximum peak at tax rate 'a', marked by a vertical dashed line down to the horizontal axis. Beyond 'a', the curve declines steeply until it returns to zero revenue at a tax rate of 100.

pg_21__page_81_Picture_1.jpeg.description: A 3D geometric diagram illustrating two concentric cubes representing volumes f(a) = a^3 and f(a + 1) = (a + 1)^3. An inner cube with solid line edges has side lengths equal to 'a', showing a side marked 'a', a front base edge marked 'a', and a depth edge marked 'a'. Surrounding it is a larger dashed cube with edges increased by 1 unit on each side. Labels show the extra length of 1 at the bottom left, the bottom right, and at the top above the inner cube's height, illustrating how increasing each edge of a cube from 'a' to 'a + 1' expands the cube's volume in three dimensions.

pg_21__page_81_Picture_3.jpeg.description: Two geometric diagrams illustrating the visual representation of volume expansion for a cube with edge length 'a'. On the left, a cube with edge length 'a' is shown inside a larger dashed cuboid extended by 1 unit along its dimensions. On the right, a cube of side length 'a' is shown with a smaller unit cube of dimensions 1 by 1 by 1 placed at one of its top corners, representing the addition of volume.

pg_21__page_83_Figure_1.jpeg.description:
A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating the concepts of domain and range for a continuous function curve labeled f. The horizontal axis is labeled x, and the vertical axis is labeled y. A blue curve f starts at a left endpoint, goes up to a local maximum, curves down to a local minimum, and then rises to a higher right endpoint.

- The domain of the function, labeled D_f, is highlighted as a light blue line segment along the x-axis, bounded by dashed vertical projection lines extending from the leftmost and rightmost points of the curve.
- The range of the function, labeled R_f, is highlighted as a light blue line segment along the y-axis, bounded by dashed horizontal projection lines extending from the lowest y-value (the start of the curve) to the highest y-value (the right endpoint of the curve).

pg_21__page_83_Figure_3.jpeg.description: A diagram illustrating a function as an engine or machine. On the left, an input arrow labeled 'x' enters the machine. On the right, an output arrow labeled 'f(x)' exits the machine.

pg_21__page_83_Picture_11.jpeg.description: An illustration of a scientific calculator featuring an electronic display screen at the top, a section of smaller function keys below the display, and a keypad layout below consisting of numeric and operational buttons.

pg_21__page_85_Figure_9.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate system diagram showing two perpendicular intersecting axes labeled 'x' (horizontal) and 'y' (vertical). Tick marks are drawn along both axes, with '1' marked one unit to the right of the origin on the x-axis and one unit above the origin on the y-axis. The four regions formed by the axes are labeled as 'Quadrant 1' (top-right), 'Quadrant 2' (top-left), 'Quadrant 3' (bottom-left), and 'Quadrant 4' (bottom-right).

pg_21__page_85_Figure_11.jpeg.description:
A Cartesian coordinate plane with labeled x-axis and y-axis, with tick marks indicating 1 unit each. Two points are plotted:
1. Point P at (3, 4) in the first quadrant, with dashed projection lines extending down to x = 3 and left to y = 4.
2. Point Q at (-5, -2) in the third quadrant, with dashed projection lines extending up to x = -5 and right to y = -2.

pg_21__page_86_Figure_12.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing a parabola opening upwards. The horizontal axis (x-axis) spans from -3 to 4, and the vertical axis (y-axis) spans from -3 to 4. Five key points are plotted on the curve: (0, 3), (1, 0), (2, -1), (3, 0), and (4, 3). The vertex of the parabola is located at (2, -1).

pg_21__page_86_Figure_14.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing a straight line plotted on an x-y plane. The horizontal x-axis ranges from -3 to 4, and the vertical y-axis ranges from -3 to 4. The line passes through several marked points with black dots: (-1, -3), (0, -1), (1, 1), and (2, 3). The y-intercept is at (0, -1) and the x-intercept is at (0.5, 0). The line has a positive slope equal to 2, corresponding to the linear equation y = 2x - 1.

pg_21__page_87_Figure_3.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating the identity function y = x. The x-axis ranges from -3 to 3, and the y-axis ranges from -3 to 3. A straight blue line passes through the origin (0, 0) and continues diagonally upward to the right and downward to the left, labeled with the equation y = x.

pg_21__page_87_Figure_5.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing the parabola y = x^2. The x-axis ranges from -3 to 3, and the y-axis ranges from -3 to 3. The curve passes through the origin (0, 0), opens upward symmetrically about the y-axis, and passes through the points (-1, 1) and (1, 1).

pg_21__page_87_Figure_7.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing the cubic function y = x^3. The x-axis ranges from -3 to 3, and the y-axis ranges from -3 to 3. The curve passes through the origin (0,0), (-1,-1), and (1,1). It flattens near the origin, extends downwards to the left into the third quadrant, and extends upwards to the right into the first quadrant.

pg_21__page_87_Figure_9.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate system showing the graph of the square root function, labeled y = sqrt(x). The x-axis ranges from -3 to 3, and the y-axis ranges from -3 to 3. The graph starts at the origin (0,0) and extends into the first quadrant as a smooth curve increasing at a decreasing rate, passing near the point (1, 1).

pg_21__page_87_Figure_11.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing the rectangular hyperbola representing the function y = 1/x. The x-axis ranges from -3 to 3 and the y-axis ranges from -3 to 3. The graph consists of two separate blue curves in opposite quadrants: one in the first quadrant passing through (1, 1) and approaching the positive x and y axes asymptotically, and one in the third quadrant passing through (-1, -1) and approaching the negative x and y axes asymptotically.

pg_21__page_87_Figure_13.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating the absolute value function, labeled y = |x|. The graph forms a V-shape with its vertex at the origin (0,0). The right branch extends through points (1,1), (2,2), and (3,3) in the first quadrant, while the left branch extends through points (-1,1), (-2,2), and (-3,3) in the second quadrant. Both x and y axes are marked with tick marks from -3 to 3.

pg_21__page_87_Figure_18.jpeg.description:
A plot of the graph of a function y = f(x) in a Cartesian coordinate system, labeled Figure 11. The x-axis ranges from -5 to 5, and the y-axis ranges from -4 to 5. Key points visible on the continuous curve include:
- At x = -5, y = 0.
- Between x = -5 and x = -2, the function drops to a local minimum near (-3, -4) and then rises back up.
- At x = -3, y is near -3.5.
- At x = -2, y = 0 (an x-intercept).
- At x = 0, y = 2 (the y-intercept).
- As x increases from 0, the curve rises to a local maximum near x = 3 where y = 4.
- At x = 3, y = 4.
- At x = 4, y = 0 (an x-intercept), where the curve terminates.

pg_21__page_88_Figure_13.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating a linear function represented by a straight blue line with equation y = ax + b (where a > 0). The line has a positive slope, rising from left to right. The y-intercept is marked on the y-axis at a distance b above the origin, indicated by a vertical double-ended arrow labeled 'b'.

pg_21__page_88_Figure_15.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating the linear function y = ax + b where a < 0. The y-axis is a vertical line and the x-axis is a horizontal line intersecting at the origin (0, 0). A line with a negative slope (slanting downwards from left to right) crosses the y-axis at a positive y-intercept marked as 'b' with a vertical double-headed arrow measuring the distance from the origin to the intercept. The line crosses the x-axis at a positive x-intercept labeled as '-b/a'.

pg_21__page_88_Figure_17.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating a horizontal line corresponding to the linear equation y = b (where a = 0). The horizontal x-axis and vertical y-axis are shown with arrows pointing in their positive directions. A cyan horizontal line is drawn parallel to the x-axis above it. A double-headed vertical arrow measures the distance from the x-axis up to the cyan line, labeled with the variable 'b'. Above the cyan line, the equation is labeled 'y = b (a = 0)'.

pg_21__page_89_Figure_8.jpeg.description:
A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating the concept of the slope of a line using similar right triangles. A blue line passes through two main points, P = (x1, y1) and Q = (x2, y2). A larger right triangle is formed below the line segment PQ with vertices at P, Q, and R = (x2, y1). The horizontal leg PR has a length of x2 - x1, and the vertical leg QR has a length of y2 - y1.

To the lower left along the same blue line, a smaller similar right triangle is shown with vertices P', Q', and R'. The horizontal base P'R' has a length of 1, and the vertical height Q'R' is labeled 'a', representing the unit rise or slope of the line, where a = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1).

pg_21__page_90_Figure_5.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing a straight line labelled l. The x-axis ranges from 0 to 6 with unit tick marks, and the y-axis ranges from -2 to 4 with unit tick marks. The line l passes through the y-intercept at (0, 1) and two labeled points: point P at coordinates (2, 2) and point Q at coordinates (4, 3). A right-angled triangle formed by dashed lines connects point P horizontally to x = 4 at y = 2, and vertically up to point Q at (4, 3), illustrating a horizontal run of 2 units (from x = 2 to x = 4) and a vertical rise of 1 unit (from y = 2 to y = 3).

pg_21__page_90_Figure_7.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing a straight line m passing through two marked points, P and Q. Point P is located at coordinates (2, 2) and point Q is located at coordinates (1, -2). A dashed line forms a right triangle by extending vertically downwards from P to y = -2 and horizontally from Q to x = 2. The x-axis is labeled from 1 to 6, and the y-axis is labeled from -2 to 4.

pg_21__page_90_Figure_9.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing a line labeled 'n' with a negative slope. The vertical axis is labeled 'y' and ranges from -2 to 4. The horizontal axis is labeled 'x' and ranges from 0 to 6. Line 'n' passes through the y-intercept at (0, 4) and the x-intercept at (4, 0). Two specific points are marked on the line: point P at coordinates (2, 2) and point Q at coordinates (5, -1). Dashed lines illustrate the horizontal and vertical distance between points P and Q, forming a right-triangle component from x = 2 to x = 5 and y = 2 to y = -1.

pg_21__page_92_Figure_3.jpeg.description:
A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating the graphical solution to a system of two linear equations. The horizontal x-axis and vertical y-axis both have tick marks spaced by 1 unit, with '1' labeled on both axes.

Two blue straight lines are plotted:
1. An increasing line labeled with the equation 'x - y = -1', passing through the y-intercept at (0, 1) and x-intercept at (-1, 0).
2. A decreasing line labeled with the equation 'x + y = 5', passing through the y-intercept at (0, 5) and x-intercept at (5, 0).

The two lines intersect at a black dot marked with the coordinates (2, 3), representing the solution to the system of linear equations.

pg_21__page_92_Figure_5.jpeg.description:
A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating the solution to a system of two linear equations by finding their point of intersection.

The two plotted lines are:
1. $3x + y = -7$, a line with a steep negative slope.
2. $x - 4y = 2$, a line with a gentle positive slope.

The two lines intersect at a single point labeled $(-2, -1)$, which represents the unique solution to the system.

pg_21__page_92_Figure_7.jpeg.description:
A Cartesian coordinate system showing two parallel line graphs with negative slopes plotted in blue.

The upper parallel line passes through the y-intercept at (0, 3) and the x-intercept at (4, 0). It is labeled with its equation: 6x + 8y = 24.

The lower parallel line passes through the y-intercept at (0, 0.5) and the x-intercept at (2/3, 0). It is labeled with its equation: 3x + 4y = 2.

The coordinate axes show tick marks at unit intervals, with x labeled at the horizontal arrow head and y at the vertical arrow head. Marks for 1 are indicated on both the positive x-axis and positive y-axis.

pg_21__page_92_Figure_15.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating the linear inequality region for $2x + y \le 4$. The graph features a solid blue line defined by the equation $2x + y = 4$, which intersects the $y$-axis at $(0, 4)$ and the $x$-axis at $(2, 0)$. The region below and to the left of this boundary line is shaded light blue, representing all coordinate points $(x, y)$ that satisfy the inequality.

pg_21__page_92_Figure_17.jpeg.description: A graph on a Cartesian coordinate plane illustrating a triangular shaded region labeled B, representing a budget set. The x-axis is labeled x and the y-axis is labeled y. The line bounding the region in the first quadrant has the equation px + qy = m. It intersects the y-axis at the point (0, m/q) and the x-axis at the point (m/p, 0). The shaded region B is bounded by the line, the y-axis (where x ≥ 0), and the x-axis (where y ≥ 0).

pg_21__page_93_Figure_9.jpeg.description:
A Cartesian coordinate system graph containing five labeled straight lines, designated as L1, L2, L3, L4, and L5, on a grid:

- The x-axis ranges from -2 to 10 and the y-axis ranges from -2 to 7.
- Line L1 passes through points such as (-1, 1), (0, 2), and (5, 7), showing a positive slope of 1.
- Line L2 passes through points such as (0, 3), (3, 1), and (8, -2), showing a negative slope of -3/5 or -0.6.
- Line L3 is a horizontal line passing through y = 1 for all x, having a slope of 0.
- Line L4 passes through points such as (4, -2), (5, 1), and (7, 7), showing a positive slope of 3.
- Line L5 passes through points such as (-1, 1.9), (0, 2), and (10, 3), showing a gentle positive slope of 0.1.

pg_21__page_96_Figure_3.jpeg.description: A line graph showing typical supply and demand curves plotted on a two-dimensional axis with quantity Q on the horizontal axis and price P on the vertical axis. The Demand curve slopes downwards from left to right, showing that demand decreases as price increases. The Supply curve slopes upwards from left to right, showing that supply increases as price increases. The two curves intersect at the equilibrium point E, which corresponds to the equilibrium price P^e on the vertical axis and the equilibrium quantity Q^e on the horizontal axis.

pg_21__page_96_Figure_5.jpeg.description: A supply and demand graph plotting Price (P) on the vertical axis against Quantity (Q) on the horizontal axis. The downward-sloping demand line is labeled P = 100 - D, starting high on the vertical axis and extending down to the horizontal axis. The upward-sloping supply line is labeled P = 1/2 S - 5, starting from a positive value on the horizontal axis. The two lines intersect at a point corresponding to an equilibrium quantity of Q = 70 and an equilibrium price of P = 30.

pg_21__page_98_Figure_6.jpeg.description:
The image shows three graphs labeled (a), (b), and (c), illustrating three typical cases of the quadratic parabola y = ax^2 + bx + c:

(a) Graph for a < 0, b^2 > 4ac: An downward-opening parabola with a maximum vertex P above the x-axis, crossing the x-axis at two distinct real roots, x_1 and x_2. The vertical dashed axis of symmetry passes through the vertex P.

(b) Graph for a > 0, b^2 < 4ac: An upward-opening parabola whose vertex P lies entirely above the x-axis, meaning it has no x-intercepts (no real roots). The vertical dashed axis of symmetry passes through vertex P.

(c) Graph for a > 0, b^2 = 4ac: An upward-opening parabola whose vertex P touches the x-axis exactly at one point (one real repeated root). The vertical dashed axis of symmetry passes through vertex P.

pg_21__page_100_Figure_12.jpeg.description: A plot showing profit (\pi) as a parabolic function of total quantity produced (Q). The horizontal axis is labeled Q and the vertical axis is labeled \pi. The curve starts at the origin (0,0), opens downwards, and reaches a maximum peak marked by a solid dot at Q = Q^M. The curve continues downwards to cross the horizontal axis at 2Q^M. To the left of the origin (Q < 0), the curve is drawn as a dashed line to indicate that negative quantities are not physically meaningful.

pg_21__page_100_Figure_14.jpeg.description: A graph plotting profit (\pi) on the vertical axis against quantity (Q) on the horizontal axis. The curve represents a profit function for a scenario where a \leq \alpha. For negative values of quantity (Q < 0), the curve is drawn as a dashed cyan parabola opening downwards with a peak in the second quadrant. It passes through the origin (0,0), labeled with a point Q^M. For positive values of quantity (Q > 0), the function continues as a solid cyan line sloping steeply downward into the fourth quadrant, indicating strictly negative profits for positive output.

pg_21__page_101_Figure_7.jpeg.description: A graph titled 'The supply curve of a perfectly competitive firm' plotting Price (P) on the vertical axis against Quantity (Q) on the horizontal axis. The curve consists of a vertical blue segment along the vertical axis from the origin (0,0) up to P = α, indicating that for prices P ≤ α, the quantity supplied Q is 0. From the point (0, α), an upward-sloping blue line extends into the first quadrant, labeled with the equation P = α + 2βQ, representing the positive quantity supplied for prices P > α.

pg_21__page_103_Diagram_2.jpeg.description: A rectangle labeled with its side lengths expressed in terms of x (Figure 5). The top and bottom horizontal sides are each labeled with the expression '250 + x'. The left and right vertical sides are each labeled with the expression '250 - x'.

pg_21__page_104_Figure_6.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing the cubic function f(x) = -x^3 + 4x^2 - x - 6. The horizontal x-axis ranges from -2 to 4, and the vertical y-axis ranges from below 0 up to 15. The blue curve enters from the top-left at x ≈ -1.8 (y ≈ 15), passes downwards through the x-intercept at x = -1, reaches a local minimum below the y-axis, crosses the y-axis at y = -6, turns upwards to pass through the x-intercept at x = 2, reaches a local maximum slightly above the x-axis, and then turns downwards through the x-intercept at x = 3, continuing into the fourth quadrant.

pg_21__page_104_Figure_8.jpeg.description: A graph plotting a cubic cost function y = C(Q) on a coordinate plane with horizontal axis Q (representing quantity) and vertical axis y (representing cost). The curve starts at a positive y-intercept on the vertical axis, curves upward while bending concave downward initially, passes through an inflection point, and then curves upward more steeply with a concave upward shape as Q increases.

pg_21__page_107_Figure_6.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing a parabola opening upwards representing a quadratic function f(x). The y-axis ranges from -2 to 2, and the x-axis ranges from -2 to 2. The parabola has its vertex at the y-intercept (0, -2) and passes through the x-intercepts at (-2, 0) and (2, 0).

pg_21__page_107_Figure_8.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing a cubic function curve y = f(x). The curve crosses the x-axis at x = -3, x = -1, and x = 2. It passes through the y-intercept at (0, -3). The local maximum is located between x = -3 and x = -1 at approximately x = -2 with y = 2. The local minimum is located between x = 0 and x = 2 at approximately x = 0.5 with y = -4.

pg_21__page_109_Figure_10.jpeg.description: A plot of the hyperbola function y = a/x in the first quadrant of a Cartesian coordinate system. A point P is marked on the curve with an x-coordinate of x_0 and a y-coordinate of a/x_0. A shaded rectangle labeled 'A' is formed between the origin (0,0), the point (x_0, 0) on the x-axis, the point P on the curve, and the point (0, a/x_0) on the y-axis, illustrating that the area of this rectangle is equal to x_0 * (a/x_0) = a.

pg_21__page_110_Figure_18.jpeg.description:
Three polynomial graphs labeled (a), (b), and (c) from Figure 6:

- **Graph (a):** A parabola opening upwards with x-intercepts at $x = -1$ and $x = 3$. The vertex (lowest point) is marked at $(1, -2)$.
- **Graph (b):** A cubic polynomial curve with x-intercepts at $x = -3$, $x = 1$, and $x = 2$. As $x \to -\infty$, $y \to +\infty$, and as $x \to +\infty$, $y \to -\infty$. The y-intercept is labeled at $(0, -12)$.
- **Graph (c):** A cubic polynomial curve with a single root at $x = -3$ and a tangent root (local minimum) at $x = 2$. The curve passes through the y-axis at $(0, 6)$. As $x \to -\infty$, $y \to -\infty$, and as $x \to +\infty$, $y \to +\infty$.

pg_21__page_111_Figure_10.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating the power function y = x^r where 0 < r < 1. The horizontal axis represents x (marked from 1 to 3) and the vertical axis represents y (marked from 1 to 3). The curve starts at the origin (0,0) and rises steeply at first, passing through the key point (1,1) indicated by dashed reference lines. As x increases beyond 1, the curve continues to increase but at a decreasing rate (concave down).

pg_21__page_111_Figure_12.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating the power function y = x^r for r > 1 in the first quadrant. The horizontal x-axis and vertical y-axis are marked with tick marks at 1, 2, and 3. The curve starts at the origin (0,0), passes through the point (1,1) (indicated by dashed vertical and horizontal lines extending to the axes), and curves upward with increasing steepness (concave up) as x increases beyond 1.

pg_21__page_111_Figure_14.jpeg.description: A graph on the Cartesian coordinate system showing a power function y = x^r with a negative exponent (r < 0) in the first quadrant. The horizontal x-axis and vertical y-axis are labeled with tick marks from 1 to 3. A blue curve decreases continuously from top-left near the y-axis, passing through the point (1, 1), marked by dashed gray lines extending to 1 on the x-axis and 1 on the y-axis, and continues flattening toward the x-axis as x increases.

pg_21__page_112_Figure_4.jpeg.description:
A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating various power functions $y = x^r$ for $x \ge 0$.

- Horizontal axis ($x$): labeled with tick marks at 1 and 2.
- Vertical axis ($y$): labeled with tick marks at 1 and 2.
- All curves pass through the origin $(0, 0)$ and intersect at the point $(1, 1)$.

Curves shown:
1. $y = x^3$: steep curve passing below other curves between $0 < x < 1$, then rising sharply above all others for $x > 1$.
2. $y = x^2$: parabolic curve positioned between $y = x^3$ and $y = x$.
3. $y = x$: a straight diagonal line passing through $(0,0)$, $(1,1)$, and $(2,2)$.
4. $y = x^{1/2}$: square root curve, positioned above $y = x$ for $0 < x < 1$ and below $y = x$ for $x > 1$.
5. $y = x^{1/3}$: cube root curve, highest curve for $0 < x < 1$ and lowest curve for $x > 1$, flattening out as $x$ increases.

pg_21__page_112_Figure_8.jpeg.description: Graph showing a square root curve starting on the x-axis at x = 2 (two tick marks to the right of the y-axis, where y = 0) and increasing gradually to the right, representing a function of the form y = sqrt(x - 2).

pg_21__page_112_Figure_10.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing a decreasing exponential curve in blue. The x-axis and y-axis intersect at the origin. The curve passes through the x-axis at x = -2 (two tick marks to the left of the origin) and through the y-axis at y = -1 (one tick mark below the origin). As x increases to the right, the curve approaches a horizontal dashed line representing a horizontal asymptote at y = -2.

pg_21__page_112_Figure_12.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing a blue parabola opening upwards. The x-axis ranges from negative values to positive values with tick marks indicating units. The parabola intersects the x-axis at x = -1 and x = 3, with its vertex below the x-axis around (1, -2). The y-axis shows tick marks above and below the x-axis, with the y-intercept at (0, -1.5).

pg_21__page_112_Figure_14.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing a smooth blue curve passing through the xy-plane. The curve starts in the second quadrant (upper left) and moves downwards and to the right, crossing the vertical y-axis at around 3.5 units above the origin, and terminating at the horizontal x-axis at x = 2. The graph includes marked grid tick marks along both the x-axis and y-axis.

pg_21__page_112_Figure_16.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing a downward-opening parabola representing a quadratic function y = f(x). The x-axis has tick marks at x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. The y-axis has tick marks at y = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2. The parabola passes through the x-intercepts at (-1, 0) and (3, 0), has a y-intercept at (0, 1.5), and its vertex is located at (1, 2).

pg_21__page_112_Figure_18.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing a continuous, increasing curve (plotted in light blue) that approaches a horizontal asymptote from below as x approaches positive infinity. The curve crosses the negative x-axis at x = -1 and the positive y-axis at y = 1. A dashed horizontal line represents the horizontal asymptote located at y = 2.

pg_21__page_113_Figure_10.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating an exponential growth function f(t) = A * a^t where a > 1. The horizontal axis is labeled t and the vertical axis is labeled y. The blue curve begins near the negative t-axis as an asymptote, increases gradually as it moves right, intersects the y-axis at point (0, A) labeled with 'A', and then rises steeply into the first quadrant. Text next to the curve reads 'f(t) = A * a^t' and '(a > 1)'.

pg_21__page_113_Figure_12.jpeg.description: A plot of the exponential decay function f(t) = A * a^t on a Cartesian coordinate system, where the horizontal axis represents t and the vertical axis represents y. The base 'a' satisfies 0 < a < 1. The curve continuously decreases from left to right, approaching the positive t-axis asymptotically as t goes to positive infinity. The curve crosses the y-axis at point A, corresponding to the initial value where t = 0 and y = A.

pg_21__page_116_Figure_9.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating two exponential functions, y = e^x and y = e^(-x). The horizontal x-axis ranges from -2 to 2, and the vertical y-axis ranges from 0 to 4. Both curves intersect the y-axis at the point (0, 1). The solid blue curve representing y = e^x increases as x increases, passing through approximately (1, 2.72). The dashed blue curve representing y = e^(-x) decreases as x increases, forming a reflection of y = e^x across the vertical y-axis.

pg_21__page_116_Picture_11.jpeg.description: A line-art illustration of a scientific pocket calculator featuring a display screen at the top and a grid of keypad buttons below.

pg_21__page_118_Figure_3.jpeg.description: A graph of an exponential function on a Cartesian coordinate plane. The y-intercept of the curve is at (0, 2). The curve passes through the marked point (2, 8) in the first quadrant and approaches the negative x-axis asymptotically.

pg_21__page_118_Figure_5.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing an exponential curve y = f(x). The graph has a horizontal x-axis and vertical y-axis. The curve passes through the second quadrant into the first quadrant, increasing rapidly. Two points are plotted and labeled on the curve: (-1, 2/3) in the second quadrant and (1, 6) in the first quadrant.

pg_21__page_118_Figure_7.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing a decreasing exponential curve labeled on the xy-plane. The y-intercept is at (0, 4), marked with a dot and labeled 4. Another point on the curve is plotted in the first quadrant at (4, 1/4), labeled with the coordinates (4, 1/4). The curve approaches the positive x-axis as x increases.

pg_21__page_121_Figure_7.jpeg.description: A plot illustrating the geometric construction of the inverse function $g(x) = \ln x$ from the exponential function $f(u) = e^u$. The horizontal axis is labeled $u$ and the vertical axis is labeled $v$. An exponential curve, labeled $f(u) = e^u$, increases as $u$ moves right and passes through the vertical intercept at $v = 1$. A point on the vertical axis labeled $x$ (where $x > 1$) extends a horizontal line with an arrow pointing right to intersect the curve at $(u, v) = (g(x), x)$. From this point on the curve, a vertical line drops down with an arrow pointing toward the horizontal axis, meeting the $u$-axis at the labeled position $g(x)$.

pg_21__page_121_Figure_9.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph plotting the natural logarithmic function g(x) = ln x. The horizontal x-axis goes from 0 to past 4, labeled with ticks at 1, 2, 3, and 4. The vertical y-axis goes from -1 to 2, with ticks at -1, 1, and 2. The curve passes through the x-intercept at (1, 0), approaches negative infinity as x approaches 0 from the right, and increases monotonically with a decreasing slope as x increases, passing through approximately (e, 1) near x = 2.72.

pg_21__page_123_Figure_14.jpeg.description:
A Cartesian coordinate graph displaying two functions labeled as $y = f(x)$ and $y = g(x)$ plotted on a grid ranging from $x = -3$ to $4$ and $y = -4$ to $6$.

- **$y = f(x)$** is a parabola (quadratic function) opening upward with a vertex at $(1, -4)$. It passes through the y-intercept $(0, -3)$, x-intercepts at $x = -1$ and $x = 3$, and passes through the point $(-2, 5)$.
- **$y = g(x)$** is a straight line (linear function) decreasing from left to right. It has a y-intercept at $(0, 3)$ and an x-intercept at $(3, 0)$. It passes through $(-2, 5)$ and $(2, 1)$.
- **Intersections**: The two graphs intersect at two points: $(-2, 5)$ and $(3, 0)$.

pg_21__page_125_Figure_2.jpeg.description: A plot of the hyperbola y = f(x) = (ax + b) / (x + c). The graph shows a vertical asymptote at a positive x-value (x = -c > 0, so c < 0) and a horizontal asymptote at a positive y-value (y = a > 0). The curve has two branches: one in the upper-right quadrant formed by the asymptotes, and one in the lower-left quadrant. The lower-left branch intersects the positive y-axis (y-intercept = b/c > 0) and the positive x-axis (x-intercept = -b/a > 0).

pg_21__page_125_Figure_4.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph displaying a upward-opening parabola labeled $y = g(x) = px^2 + qx + r$. The parabola opens upward (meaning $p > 0$), has its vertex located in the fourth quadrant (where $x > 0$ and $y < 0$), crosses the negative $y$-axis (meaning $r < 0$), and intersects the $x$-axis at two distinct real roots (one negative and one positive, with the positive root having a larger absolute value).

pg_21__page_127_Figure_4.jpeg.description:
A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating vertical shifts of the square root function y = sqrt(x). The graph displays three blue curves plotted for x >= 0:
1. The middle curve represents the parent function y = sqrt(x), starting at the origin (0, 0) and passing through points such as (1, 1) and (4, 2).
2. The top curve represents y = sqrt(x) + 2, shifted upwards by 2 units, starting at (0, 2) and passing through (1, 3) and (4, 4).
3. The bottom curve represents y = sqrt(x) - 2, shifted downwards by 2 units, starting at (0, -2), crossing the x-axis at (4, 0), and passing through (1, -1).

pg_21__page_127_Figure_6.jpeg.description:
A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating horizontal shifts of the square root function y = sqrt(x).

The coordinate system displays the x-axis ranging from -2 to 5 and the y-axis ranging from -2 to 4.

Three curves (in blue) are plotted:
1. The base function, y = sqrt(x), starting at the origin (0,0) and curving upward to the right, passing near (1,1) and terminating around (3.5, 1.8).
2. The left-shifted function, y = sqrt(x + 2), starting at (-2,0), passing through the y-intercept at (0, sqrt(2) ≈ 1.41), and continuing upward to the right.
3. The right-shifted function, y = sqrt(x - 2), starting at (2,0) and curving upward to the right through x = 5.

pg_21__page_127_Figure_8.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating vertical stretching of a square root function on the interval x from 0 to 5. The base graph is labeled y = \sqrt{x}, passing through (0,0), (1,1), and (4,2). Above it, the vertically stretched graph is labeled y = 2\sqrt{x}, passing through (0,0), (1,2), and (4,4), showing that each y-value of the base function is multiplied by a factor of 2.

pg_21__page_127_Figure_10.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing two curves originating from the origin (0,0). The upper branch, represented by a dashed blue line opening to the right, is labeled $y = \sqrt{x}$. The lower branch, represented by a solid blue line extending into the fourth quadrant, is labeled $y = -\sqrt{x}$. Together, these two square root functions form a horizontal parabola opening to the right.

pg_21__page_127_Figure_12.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating two reflection/square root function curves. On the right, for x >= 0, a dashed blue curve representing y = sqrt(x) starts at the origin (0,0) and passes through approximately (1,1) and (4,2) up to x = 5. On the left, for x <= 0, a solid blue curve representing y = sqrt(-x) starts at the origin (0,0) and extends to the left, passing through (-1,1) and (-4,2) up to x = -5. This demonstrates a horizontal reflection across the y-axis.

pg_21__page_128_Figure_10.jpeg.description:
A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating the step-by-step transformation of the parabola y = x^2 to y = 2 - (x + 2)^2. 

1. The base curve y = x^2 is shown as a dashed cyan parabola opening upward with its vertex at the origin (0,0).
2. Reflecting y = x^2 across the x-axis yields y = -x^2, shown as a dashed cyan parabola opening downward with its vertex at (0,0).
3. Translating y = -x^2 left by 2 units gives y = -(x + 2)^2, shown as a dashed cyan parabola with its vertex at (-2, 0).
4. Translating y = -(x + 2)^2 upward by 2 units yields the final solid cyan curve y = 2 - (x + 2)^2, which is a downward-opening parabola with its vertex at (-2, 1) [noting the vertical scale shows 1 unit above the origin]. 

Key axis labels include x-ticks at -4, -2, 2 and y-ticks at -2, -1, 1, 2.

pg_21__page_128_Figure_12.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating two rational functions. A solid blue curve represents the function y = 1/(x - 2) + 3, with a vertical asymptote at x = 2 (vertical dashed line) and a horizontal asymptote at y = 3 (horizontal dashed line). The graph has two branches: one in the upper-right quadrant approaching the asymptotes, and one in the lower-left region passing through (0, 2.5) and intersecting the x-axis around x = 1.67. Additionally, a dashed blue curve is shown, representing the parent function y = 1/x before transformations, with its vertical asymptote at x = 0 (the y-axis) and horizontal asymptote at y = 0 (the x-axis).

pg_21__page_129_Figure_2.jpeg.description: A supply and demand graph plotting price (P) on the vertical axis against quantity (Q, D, S) on the horizontal axis. The downward-sloping demand curve is labeled D = 100 - P. The original upward-sloping supply curve is labeled S = 10 + 2P, intersecting the demand curve at the original equilibrium point corresponding to a price of 30 and quantity of 70. A shifted supply curve to the right is labeled \tilde{S} = 16 + 2P, intersecting the demand curve at a new equilibrium point corresponding to a lower price of 28 and a higher quantity of 72.

pg_21__page_129_Figure_4.jpeg.description: A supply and demand graph displaying price (P) on the vertical axis and quantity (Q, D, S) on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping demand curve is labeled $D = a - bP$. There are two upward-sloping parallel supply curves: the original supply curve $S = \alpha + \beta P$ and a shifted supply curve to its right, $\tilde{S} = \tilde{\alpha} + \beta P$. The intersection of $D$ and $S$ determines the original equilibrium point with price $P^e$ and quantity $Q^e$. The shift in supply results in a new equilibrium at the intersection of $D$ and $\tilde{S}$, characterized by a lower equilibrium price $\tilde{P}^e$ and a higher equilibrium quantity $\tilde{Q}^e$.

pg_21__page_130_Figure_4.jpeg.description:
A graph illustrating three tax functions plotted on a Cartesian coordinate system with 'Income (y)' on the horizontal axis and 'Tax (T)' on the vertical axis.

- The top curve represents the baseline tax function, labeled $T = f(y)$, which is strictly increasing and convex.
- The bottom curve represents the tax credit proposal, labeled $T_2 = f(y) - c$, which is a vertical downward shift of $T = f(y)$ by a distance $c$.
- The middle curve represents the income deduction proposal, labeled $T_1 = f(y - d)$, which is a horizontal rightward shift of $T = f(y)$ by a distance $d$.
- The curves $T_1$ and $T_2$ intersect at a specific income level labeled $y^*$ on the horizontal axis, representing the point where both proposals result in the exact same tax liability.

pg_21__page_131_Figure_1.jpeg.description: A coordinate graph labeled Figure 11 showing a continuous curve y = f(x). The graph has a relative minimum tangent to the x-axis at (-2, 0), rises to a local maximum on the y-axis at (0, 2), and then passes down through the x-intercept at (1, 0) as it continues downward into the fourth quadrant.

pg_21__page_131_Figure_6.jpeg.description: The image contains three line graphs illustrating student enrollment from 1986 to 1997, labeled as Figure 1. On the left side, there are two separate plots: the top plot shows the curve f(t) representing female enrollment with the area under the curve shaded; the bottom plot shows the curve m(t) representing male enrollment with the area under the curve shaded. On the right side, a combined stacked area graph is shown with vertical axis 'Number in thousands' (ranging from 0 to 100) and horizontal axis 'Year' (from 86 to 97). The lower region under curve m(t) is labeled 'Male' (starting at approximately 20 in '86 and rising to around 40 in '97). Stacked above m(t) is the curve m(t) + f(t), with the region between m(t) and m(t) + f(t) labeled 'Female' (starting around 40 total and reaching around 85 total in '97).

pg_21__page_132_Figure_10.jpeg.description:
Three side-by-side Cartesian coordinate graphs illustrating how the average cost function A(Q) is formed by adding a quadratic function and a hyperbola.

1. Left graph: Shows a parabolic curve opening upwards, with the vertical distance from the horizontal axis Q to the curve labeled as aQ^2 + bQ + c.
2. Middle graph: Shows a hyperbola decreasing towards the horizontal axis Q as Q increases, with the vertical height labeled as d/Q.
3. Right graph: Shows the combined graph A(Q) as a solid curve with a U-shape. Below it, the two component curves (aQ^2 + bQ + c and d/Q) are drawn with dashed lines. Vertical arrows demonstrate that at a given point Q, the height of A(Q) is equal to the sum of the vertical distances d/Q and aQ^2 + bQ + c.

pg_21__page_133_Figure_1.jpeg.description:
A graph plotting three functions against quantity Q on the horizontal axis and value y on the vertical axis:
1. Revenue function R(Q): A straight line passing through the origin with a constant positive slope.
2. Cost function C(Q): A curve starting at a positive y-intercept (fixed cost) that is convex and increases at an increasing rate, intersecting R(Q) at two points.
3. Profit function \pi(Q) = R(Q) - C(Q): An inverted U-shaped curve starting below the horizontal axis (at negative fixed cost). It crosses the Q-axis at the two intersection points of R(Q) and C(Q) (break-even points) and reaches its maximum value at Q^*, which corresponds to the point where the vertical distance between R(Q) and C(Q) is greatest.

pg_21__page_134_Picture_2.jpeg.description: An illustration of a scientific electronic calculator featuring a top display screen, two rows of black function keys near the top, a grid of white number keys, and a column of black operation keys on the right side.

pg_21__page_135_Figure_3.jpeg.description: A plot showing the graph of an even function f on a Cartesian coordinate plane. The graph of f is a continuous curve that is symmetric about the vertical y-axis. Dashed vertical lines extend from the x-axis at points -x and x up to the curve, illustrating that the function values at -x and x are equal, i.e., f(-x) = f(x).

pg_21__page_135_Figure_5.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating an odd function $f$ that is symmetric about the origin. The function passes through the origin $(0,0)$. For a positive value $x$ on the horizontal axis, a dashed vertical line connects to a point in the first quadrant with positive $y$-value $f(x)$. For the corresponding negative value $-x$, a dashed vertical line connects to a point in the third quadrant with negative $y$-value $f(-x)$, demonstrating $f(-x) = -f(x)$.

pg_21__page_135_Figure_7.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating symmetry about the vertical line x = a for a function f. The curve f is continuous and wave-like, symmetric about a solid vertical line passing through the x-axis at x = a, which aligns with a local maximum of f. Two vertical dashed lines dropped from the curve intersect the x-axis at equidistant points x = a - x and x = a + x, showing that the function values at these two points are equal, i.e., f(a - x) = f(a + x).

pg_21__page_136_Figure_11.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating a one-to-one function f. The horizontal axis is labeled x, and the vertical axis is labeled y. On the x-axis, an interval set labeled A is highlighted. Dotted vertical lines extend from the endpoints of interval A up to the graph of the blue curve f, which is strictly increasing. Dotted horizontal lines then extend from the endpoints of the curve to the y-axis, mapping interval A on the x-axis directly to a highlighted vertical interval labeled f(A) = B on the y-axis, demonstrating the range B corresponding to the domain A.

pg_21__page_136_Figure_13.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating a function g(x) that is not one-to-one on the interval A. The function curve g rises from the left, reaches a local maximum, falls to a local minimum, and then turns upward again. A horizontal dashed line at y = y1 intersects the graph of g at two distinct points corresponding to inputs x1 and x2 on the x-axis, showing that g(x1) = g(x2) = y1 for x1 ≠ x2 within the shaded domain interval A.

pg_21__page_138_Figure_10.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating the geometric relationship between two inverse functions across the line y = x. The x-axis ranges from -4 to 10 and the y-axis ranges from -4 to 8. A dashed diagonal line represents y = x. A solid blue line depicts f(x) = 4x - 3, passing through points (0, -3), (1, 1), and (2, 5). A second solid blue line depicts its inverse, g(x) = 1/4 x + 3/4, passing through points (-3, 0), (1, 1), and (5, 2). The two function lines intersect each other and the line y = x at the point (1, 1). A double-ended arrow orthogonal to the line y = x highlights the reflection symmetry between f(x) and g(x).

pg_21__page_138_Figure_12.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating two inverse functions, f(x) and g(x), reflected across the line y = x. The x-axis ranges from -2 to around 4, and the y-axis ranges from -2 to over 3. The line y = x is drawn as a dashed line passing through the origin. The function g(x) = x^5 - 1 is shown as a steep blue curve passing through (0, -1) and (1, 0). The function f(x) = (x + 1)^(1/5) is shown as a blue curve passing through (-1, 0) and (0, 1). The two curves intersect with each other and the line y = x at approximately (1.17, 1.17). A double-headed arrow perpendicular to y = x highlights the reflection symmetry between the two curves.

pg_21__page_139_Picture_5.jpeg.description: A simplified line drawing of a scientific calculator showing a display screen at the top, two rows of black control buttons below the screen, and a keypad layout below containing white numerical/function keys and a rightmost column of black function keys.

pg_21__page_140_Figure_2.jpeg.description:
A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating two inverse functions, f(x) and g(x), reflected across the line y = x.

Key details:
- The dashed line represents y = x, passing through the origin.
- The function f(x) = sqrt(3x + 9) starts at x = -3 on the x-axis, passes through the y-intercept at (0, 3), and curves upward to the right into the first quadrant.
- The function g(x) = (1/3)x^2 - 3 (for x >= 0) starts at the y-intercept (0, -3), passes through the x-intercept at (3, 0), and curves steeply upward into the first quadrant.
- The two curves intersect with each other and the dashed line y = x in the first quadrant.

pg_21__page_142_Figure_11.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing the curve of the equation x * sqrt(y) = 2 in the first quadrant. The horizontal axis x and vertical axis y are both labeled from 0 to 6 with increments of 2. The blue curve decreases rapidly as x increases. Four specific points are plotted with black dots along the curve: at x = 1, y = 4; at x = 2, y = 1; at x = 4, y = 0.25; and at x = 6, y = 1/9 (approximately 0.11).

pg_21__page_142_Figure_13.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph displaying a circle centered at the origin (0, 0) labeled with the equation x^2 + y^2 = 16. The x-axis and y-axis are marked from -4 to 4 with tick marks every 1 unit, labeled at -2 and 2 on both axes. The circle intersects the axes at (4, 0), (-4, 0), (0, 4), and (0, -4). Several points along the circle are highlighted with black dots, showing symmetry across both axes.

pg_21__page_142_Figure_15.jpeg.description: A graph on a Cartesian coordinate plane showing a bell-shaped curve. The horizontal axis (x-axis) ranges from -4 to 4, and the vertical axis (y-axis) ranges from 0 to 3. The peak of the curve is symmetric about the y-axis, reaching a maximum height around y = 2.3 at x = 0. As x moves further away from 0 in both positive and negative directions, the curve decreases smoothly towards the x-axis, approaching y = 0 as an asymptote.

pg_21__page_143_Figure_9.jpeg.description: A graph on a Cartesian coordinate system showing a smooth, wave-like blue curve plotted against the x and y axes. A vertical line intersects the curve at a single point, illustrating the vertical-line test where a vertical line crosses the graph of a valid function at most once.

pg_21__page_143_Figure_11.jpeg.description: A plot on Cartesian axes showing a horizontal parabola opening to the right in the first quadrant. A vertical line intersects the parabola at two distinct points, illustrating the vertical-line test for a relation that is not a function.

pg_21__page_144_Figure_3.jpeg.description:
Two line graphs side-by-side labeled Figure 6, illustrating how changing the y-axis scale affects the visual perception of the same data.

Left Graph:
- Vertical Axis: 'Consump. (in billion dollars)' ranging from 3.5 to 6.5 with increments of 0.5.
- Horizontal Axis: 'Year' labeled from 68 to 74.
- Content: A steep blue line connecting data points from year 68 at ~3.55 to year 74 at ~6.8, giving the visual impression of rapid growth due to a truncated vertical axis starting at 3.5.

Right Graph:
- Vertical Axis: 'Consump. (in billion dollars)' ranging from 1.0 to 6.0 with increments of 1.0.
- Horizontal Axis: 'Year' labeled from 68 to 74.
- Content: The exact same data points plotted against a wider vertical scale starting nearer to zero, resulting in a line with a much flatter, more moderate slope.

pg_21__page_144_Figure_11.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating a piecewise function. For x <= 0, the graph is a line with a negative slope passing through (-1, 1) to the origin (0, 0). For 0 < x <= 1, the function curves upward like a parabola from (0, 0) to a filled endpoint at (1, 1). To the right of x = 1, above the point (1, 1) near y = 1.5, a blue horizontal arrow points to the left towards x = 1, indicating a jump discontinuity or a separate segment at x > 1.

pg_21__page_144_Figure_13.jpeg.description: A line graph titled 'Tax ($1000)' on the vertical axis versus 'Income ($1000)' on the horizontal axis. The vertical axis ranges from 0 to 15 in increments of 5, and the horizontal axis ranges from 0 to 70 in increments of 10. The graph consists of two connected straight line segments showing a piecewise function: the first segment starts at the origin (0, 0) and extends upward through a plotted point near (7, 1) up to a point at (29, 4). From (29, 4), a steeper second line segment goes upward and rightward towards approximately (70, 14).

pg_21__page_145_Figure_8.jpeg.description: A diagram illustrating the distance formula between two points in a Cartesian coordinate system. Axis x is horizontal and axis y is vertical. Two points are plotted: P_1 = (x_1, y_1) at the lower-left end and P_2 = (x_2, y_2) at the upper-right end, connected by a blue line segment labeled d representing the distance. A right-angled triangle is formed using dashed vertical and horizontal auxiliary lines. The horizontal leg has length x_2 - x_1 (indicated by a dimension line below), and the vertical leg has length y_2 - y_1 (indicated by a dimension line to the right).

pg_21__page_145_Figure_10.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating the line segment between two points, P1 and P2. Point P1 is located at (-4, 3) in the second quadrant, and Point P2 is located at (5, -1) in the fourth quadrant. A solid blue line segment connects P1 directly to P2. Dashed gray construction lines project vertically down from P1 to y = -1 and horizontally left from P2 to x = -4, forming a right-angled triangle below the line segment to illustrate the horizontal distance (delta x = 9) and vertical distance (delta y = 4) between the points.

pg_21__page_147_Figure_1.jpeg.description: A diagram of a circle in a Cartesian coordinate system with x and y axes. The center of the circle is marked at point (a, b). A point on the circumference of the circle is labeled (x, y). A straight line segment representing the radius r connects the center (a, b) to the point (x, y).

pg_21__page_147_Figure_3.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating a circle plotted on the x-y plane. The circle is centered at the point (-4, 1), marked by a solid black dot. A line segment representing the radius extends from the center (-4, 1) to a point on the circle's boundary, labeled with a length of 3. The circle passes through x = -1 on the horizontal axis and extends vertically from y = -2 to y = 4, with its leftmost point reaching x = -7.

pg_21__page_147_Figure_16.jpeg.description: A diagram of an ellipse in a Cartesian coordinate system (x, y axes). The center of the ellipse is located at the coordinates (x_0, y_0), marked by the intersection of dashed horizontal and vertical lines originating from x_0 on the x-axis and y_0 on the y-axis. The horizontal semi-major axis length is labeled 'a', extending from the center to the right edge of the ellipse along the horizontal axis symmetry line. The vertical semi-minor axis length is labeled 'b', extending from the center to the top edge of the ellipse along the vertical axis symmetry line. A point on the upper-right boundary of the ellipse is marked with a black dot and labeled with coordinates (x, y).

pg_21__page_147_Figure_18.jpeg.description: A graph illustrating a hyperbola opening horizontally with center at (x_0, y_0). The axes are labeled x and y. Dashed vertical line x = x_0 and horizontal line y = y_0 intersect at the center (x_0, y_0). A central dashed rectangle of width 2a and height 2b is centered at (x_0, y_0), showing semi-major axis length 'a' along the horizontal direction from the center to a vertex, and semi-minor axis length 'b' along the vertical direction. Two dashed asymptotic lines pass diagonally through the corners of the rectangle and the center (x_0, y_0). The blue hyperbola branches open to the left and right, with vertices touching the middle of the left and right sides of the central rectangle and approaching the asymptotes as they extend outwards.

pg_21__page_147_Figure_20.jpeg.description: A mathematical graph showing a vertical hyperbola centered at $(x_0, y_0)$ with light blue curves opening upward and downward. The center point $(x_0, y_0)$ is marked by dashed projection lines from the $x$-axis and $y$-axis. Two dashed diagonal asymptotic lines intersect at the center $(x_0, y_0)$. A central rectangle defined by dashed lines extends horizontally by a distance $a$ to the left of $x_0$ and vertically by a distance $b$ above $y_0$. The vertices of the hyperbola are located at $(x_0, y_0 + b)$ and $(x_0, y_0 - b)$ along the vertical line of symmetry.

pg_171__page_0_Diagram_11.jpeg.description: A Venn-like mapping diagram illustrating a function $f$ from set $A$ to set $B$. Set $A$ is represented by a large circle on the left labeled $A$ at the top, containing a point labeled $x$. Set $B$ is represented by a large circle on the right labeled $B$ at the top, containing a point labeled $f(x)$. A curved arrow labeled $f$ originates from point $x$ in set $A$ and points to $f(x)$ in set $B$.

pg_171__page_4_Figure_11.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate grid showing the graph of a curve $y = f(x)$ and a tangent line $L$ at point $P$. Point $P$ is located at $(a, f(a))$, which is 4 units to the right of the y-axis and 3 units above the x-axis (where each grid square represents 1 unit by 1 unit). The tangent line $L$ passes through point $P(4, 3)$ and another grid intersection at $(8, 5)$, giving it a slope of $\frac{5-3}{8-4} = \frac{2}{4} = \frac{1}{2}$. The blue curve $y = f(x)$ passes through $P$, reaches a local maximum further to the right, and then slopes downward.

pg_171__page_5_Figure_7.jpeg.description:
A Cartesian coordinate graph showing a curve y = f(x) with grid lines. The x-axis ranges from 0 to 8, and the y-axis ranges from 0 to 4. 

Three points with tangent lines are plotted on the curve:
1. Point P is located at (1, 2) where the curve has a positive slope. The tangent line passes through (0, 1) and (1, 2).
2. Point Q is located at the local maximum (4, 3) where the tangent line is horizontal (slope = 0).
3. Point R is located at (7, 2.5) where the curve has a negative slope.

pg_171__page_5_Figure_12.jpeg.description: A line graph showing a curve y = f(x) and a tangent line at x = 3. The x-axis ranges from 0 to 8, and the y-axis ranges from 0 to 4. The curve y = f(x) passes through the point (3, 2). The tangent line passes through the point (3, 2) as well as the points (0, 3) and (6, 1), showing a negative slope.

pg_171__page_5_Figure_14.jpeg.description:
A Cartesian coordinate graph showing a curve $y = g(x)$ in light blue and a tangent line in black. The x-axis ranges from 0 to 8 with grid lines spaced by 1 unit. The y-axis ranges from 0 to 4 with grid lines spaced by 1 unit.

The blue curve $y = g(x)$ has a local minimum near $x = 3.8$ where $y \approx 0.4$. As $x$ increases, the curve passes through the point $(5, 1)$ where a black tangent line touches the curve. The tangent line passes through the points $(4, 0)$, $(5, 1)$, $(6, 2)$, and $(7, 3)$, showing a slope of $1$. Beyond $x = 5$, the curve rises more steeply, reaching $y = 2$ at $x = 6$ and $y \approx 3.4$ at $x = 6.5$.

pg_171__page_6_Figure_4.jpeg.description: A graph on a Cartesian coordinate plane with an x-axis and a y-axis in the first quadrant. A continuous curve in blue starts near the origin, rises steeply, passes through point P, reaches a local maximum, and then curves downward, passing through point Q. A secant line passes through both points P and Q on the curve. A tangent line labeled T touches the curve at point P and extends upward with a steeper slope than the secant line PQ.

pg_171__page_6_Figure_6.jpeg.description: A graph on a Cartesian coordinate plane illustrating how secant lines approach a tangent line at a point on a curve. A blue curve passes through a fixed point P in the first quadrant. Several points (including point Q) are marked on the curve to the right of P. Straight lines (secant lines) are drawn from point P through each of these points on the curve. An arrow indicates the movement of point Q along the curve toward point P from right to left. A line labeled T touches the curve at point P, representing the tangent line that the secant lines approach as point Q moves closer to point P.

pg_171__page_6_Figure_9.jpeg.description: A graph in the xy-plane illustrating the geometric definition of a tangent line using secant lines. A curve labeled $f$ passes through point $P = (a, f(a))$ and point $Q = (a + h, f(a + h))$. A secant line connects $P$ and $Q$. A right triangle is formed beneath the secant line with a horizontal dashed base of length $h$ and a vertical dashed height of $f(a + h) - f(a)$. A tangent line labeled $T$ touches the curve at point $P$, representing the limit of the secant line as $Q$ approaches $P$ (or as $h$ approaches 0).

pg_171__page_8_Figure_6.jpeg.description: A graph illustrating the geometric interpretation of the secant line and the difference quotient for the function f(x) = x^2. The x-axis and y-axis intersect at the origin. A blue parabolic curve representing f(x) = x^2 passes through the origin and extends upwards into the first quadrant. Two points are highlighted on the curve: point P at x = a and point Q at x = a + h. A black secant line passes through both points P and Q. A right triangle is formed using dashed lines between P and Q, where the horizontal leg along x has length h (from x = a to x = a + h), and the vertical leg has length (a + h)^2 - a^2 = 2ah + h^2, representing the change in y between P and Q.

pg_171__page_8_Figure_8.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating the function f(x) = x^2 plotted as a blue parabola opening upwards with its vertex at the origin (0,0). Two tangent lines are drawn intersecting the parabola at specific points marked with black dots. One tangent line touches the curve on the left side at x = -1, passing through (-1, 1) and extending downward through the y-axis below zero (intercepting near y = -1). The other tangent line touches the curve on the right side at x = 0.5 (passing through (0.5, 0.25)) and extends diagonally upwards to the right and downwards to the left through the y-axis near y = -0.25. The axes are labeled with x from -2 to 2 and y from -1 to 4.

pg_171__page_11_Figure_14.jpeg.description:
A graph of a continuous function y = f(x) plotted on a Cartesian coordinate system. On the x-axis, four points are marked: a, b, c, and d from left to right. 
- At x = a, the function crosses the x-axis going downward (strictly decreasing with a negative slope).
- At x = b, the function reaches a local minimum below the x-axis (horizontal tangent, slope = 0).
- At x = c, the function is strictly increasing as it passes above the x-axis (positive slope).
- At x = d, the function reaches a local maximum above the x-axis (horizontal tangent, slope = 0).

pg_171__page_12_Figure_8.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating a piece-wise or non-monotonic function behavior on the x-y plane. An arrow pointing to the right indicates direction along the x-axis, while a curve starts with a solid blue dot in the first quadrant and curves upwards as x increases, representing an increasing function segment.

pg_171__page_12_Figure_10.jpeg.description: A 2D coordinate plot with an x-axis and a y-axis. A single curve is shown in light blue, starting near the bottom left (above the x-axis) and strictly increasing to the top right. The curve starts with a concave-up shape, reaches an inflection point near the middle, and transitions to a concave-down shape as it flattens toward the top right, forming an S-shaped curve (logistic or sigmoidal shape).

pg_171__page_12_Figure_12.jpeg.description: A 2D Cartesian coordinate plot showing a function y = f(x) with axes x and y. The graph consists of a blue line segment that starts in the upper left, remains horizontal (constant value of y) as x increases, and then turns downward, sloping linearly to the right with a negative gradient.

pg_171__page_12_Figure_14.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph with x and y axes in the first quadrant. A continuous curve in blue starts near the top left with a horizontal tangent, decreases as it moves to the right, changing concavity from concave down to concave up, and flattens out near the bottom right with another horizontal tangent. The curve represents a strictly decreasing function.

pg_171__page_13_Figure_5.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing the function f(x) = -1/3 * x^3 + 2x^2 - 3x + 1. The vertical y-axis is marked from 0 to 3, and the horizontal x-axis is marked from 1 to 4. The curve crosses the y-axis at y = 1, decreases to a local minimum at x = 1 (where y = -1/3), increases to a local maximum at x = 3 (where y = 1), and then decreases as x goes beyond 3, passing through the x-axis around x ≈ 3.84.

pg_171__page_16_Figure_9.jpeg.description: A scatter plot titled 'Unemployment' showing discrete data points plotted as cross marks ('x') against time $t$ on the horizontal axis for the years 1928 and 1929. The vertical axis represents the number of unemployed individuals, with tick marks labeled at 10 000, 20 000, and 30 000. The data exhibits a distinct seasonal pattern with periodic fluctuations over time, dropping from near 28 000 at the start of 1928 down to around 15 000 mid-year, rising back up to around 24 000, dropping again to approximately 12 000 in mid-1929, and rising back above 20 000 towards the end of 1929.

pg_171__page_16_Figure_11.jpeg.description: A line plot titled "Unemployment" showing monthly unemployment data in Norway from 1928 to 1929. The vertical axis represents unemployment numbers, ranging from 10,000 to 30,000 in increments of 10,000. The horizontal axis represents time $t$, with tick marks corresponding to months throughout the years 1928 and 1929. Black 'x' symbols mark discrete data points showing seasonal fluctuations: high unemployment near 28,000-29,000 at the start of 1928, dropping to around 15,000 in mid-1928, rising back to around 24,000 by early 1929, dropping to around 12,000 in mid-1929, and rising again toward late 1929. A smooth blue trend curve fits through the data points.

pg_171__page_18_Figure_14.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph displaying the function F(x) = (e^x - 1) / x. The horizontal x-axis ranges from roughly -2 to 2, with tick marks at -2, -1, 1, and 2. The vertical y-axis ranges from 0 to 3, with tick marks at 1, 2, and 3. The curve is smooth and increasing from left to right, starting near y = 0.25 at x = -1.75, passing through an open circle at (0, 1) to indicate a point discontinuity (removable singularity) where x = 0 is undefined, and continuing upward past y = 2 near x = 1.3 to almost y = 3 at x = 1.8.

pg_171__page_24_Figure_6.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating a constant function. The x-axis and y-axis are shown with an intersection at the origin. A horizontal blue line above the x-axis represents the function labeled f(x) = A, indicating that the function value remains constant at A for all values of x.

pg_171__page_24_Figure_8.jpeg.description: A graph on a Cartesian coordinate system illustrating the geometric interpretation of adding a constant to a function, $y = f(x)$ and $y = A + f(x)$. The lower blue curve represents $y = f(x)$, and the upper blue curve represents $y = A + f(x)$, which is vertically shifted upwards by a distance $A$. A double-headed vertical arrow labeled $A$ shows the constant distance between the two curves. At a given point $x$ on the horizontal axis, a vertical dashed line connects the corresponding points on both curves. Parallel tangent lines are drawn at these points on both curves, visually demonstrating that the slope (derivative) of $y = A + f(x)$ is identical to the slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x$, because the derivative of the constant $A$ is zero.

pg_171__page_39_Figure_2.jpeg.description: A graph showing a convex curve labeled y = f(x) on a Cartesian coordinate system with positive x and y axes. As the curve goes from left to right, three short tangent lines are drawn at different points: the first tangent line on the left has a negative slope, the second at the local minimum is horizontal with zero slope, and the third on the right has a positive slope. This illustrates how the tangent line rotates counterclockwise as x increases along a convex function.

pg_171__page_39_Figure_4.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating a concave function curve labeled y = g(x) in the first quadrant. Along the curve from left to right, four short tangent lines are drawn at various points. The slopes of these tangent lines decrease as x increases, transitioning from a steep positive slope at the lower left, to a smaller positive slope, to a horizontal slope near the peak, and finally to a negative slope on the right side.

pg_171__page_39_Figure_9.jpeg.description:
Figure 3 illustrates four distinct curve types plotted on Cartesian coordinates with axes x and y:
1. 'Increasing, convex': A curve starting at a low y-value on the left and curving upwards increasingly steeply as x increases.
2. 'Increasing, concave': A curve starting at a low y-value with a steep slope on the left and flattening out as it rises to the right.
3. 'Decreasing, convex': A curve starting at a high y-value on the left, dropping steeply at first, and flattening out as x increases.
4. 'Decreasing, concave': A curve starting at a high y-value on the left with a relatively flat slope, dropping increasingly steeply as x increases.

pg_171__page_40_Figure_3.jpeg.description: A line graph showing the world population in billions from before 1600 to nearly 2000 as an example of a convex (exponentially increasing) function. The horizontal axis represents the 'year' with tick marks at 1600, 1700, 1800, 1900, and 2000. The vertical axis represents 'World pop. (billions)' with tick marks at 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5. The blue curve begins near 0 around 1500–1600, increases slowly until around 1800, and then bends upward rapidly, reaching approximately 5 billion near the year 1990–2000.

pg_171__page_40_Figure_5.jpeg.description: A graph plotting wheat yield Y against nitrogen application N. The vertical axis represents Y, with tick marks labeled 20, 40, and 60. The horizontal axis represents N, with tick marks labeled 50, 100, 150, 200, and 250. A blue concave curve rises from approximately N = 25 up through (50, 20) and (100, 35) to reach a maximum point near Y = 43 at N_0 (located between 150 and 200, around N = 175). After N_0, the curve slopes gently downward towards N = 250.

pg_171__page_40_Figure_11.jpeg.description: A line graph showing a strictly concave function in the first quadrant. The vertical axis is labeled 'Y' and the horizontal axis is labeled 'K'. A blue curve starts at the origin and rises with a decreasing slope as K increases, moving up and to the right. Text next to the curve indicates the function equation: 'Y = A K^a' with the condition '(0 < a < 1)'.

pg_171__page_40_Figure_13.jpeg.description: A graph titled 'Figure 7 Convex production function' displaying a coordinate system with capital K on the horizontal axis and output Y on the vertical axis. A blue curve starting at the origin slopes upward with increasing steepness (convex curve), representing the function Y = A * K^a with the condition (a > 1).

pg_171__page_46_Figure_36.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing the function $g(x) = \ln x$. The horizontal axis is labeled $x$ with tick marks at 1, 2, 3, and 4. The vertical axis is labeled $y$ with tick marks at -1, 1, and 2. The curve passes through the x-intercept at $(1, 0)$, continues upward into the first quadrant gradually flattening out as $x$ increases, and approaches negative infinity vertically near the y-axis ($x = 0$) in the fourth quadrant.

pg_171__page_55_Figure_4.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating the curve xy = 5 for x > 0 in the first quadrant. The horizontal axis x and vertical axis y are both labeled from 1 to 5. A hyperbola branch in cyan decreases from near (1, 5) down towards (5, 1). A point is marked on the curve at x = 3, y = 5/3 (approximately 1.67), and a tangent line is drawn through this point.

pg_171__page_56_Figure_4.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph displaying a bell-shaped curve plotted in light blue. The horizontal x-axis ranges from -4 to 4, and the vertical y-axis includes tick marks at 1 and 2. The curve has a peak slightly above y = 2 at x = 0 and is symmetric about the y-axis, flattening out asymptotically towards y = 0 as x approaches positive and negative infinity. A black tangent line is drawn at a point on the curve located at (2, 1), marked with a solid black dot. The tangent line extends roughly from x = 1, y = 1.8 down to x = 3, y = 0.1, showing a negative slope.

pg_171__page_59_Figure_5.jpeg.description: A plot on a Cartesian coordinate plane showing a lemniscate curve shaped like an infinity symbol (∞) centered at the origin (0,0). The curve extends horizontally along the x-axis with x-intercepts at -a and a, symmetric across both the x-axis and y-axis.

pg_171__page_62_Figure_1.jpeg.description: A line graph showing economic supply and demand curves with quantity Q on the horizontal axis and price P on the vertical axis. An upward-sloping supply curve is labeled Q = g(P). Two downward-sloping demand curves are shown: the original demand curve labeled Q = f(P) and a shifted demand curve labeled Q = f(P + t) located below and to the left of the original. The original equilibrium point E is located at the intersection of Q = g(P) and Q = f(P). The new equilibrium point E' is located lower and to the left on the supply curve, at the intersection of Q = g(P) and Q = f(P + t), illustrating a decrease in both equilibrium price P and quantity Q after a tax t is introduced.

pg_171__page_64_Figure_4.jpeg.description:
A Cartesian coordinate graph displaying two inverse functions, labeled f and g, reflected across the dashed line y = x.

- The horizontal axis is labeled x and the vertical axis is labeled y.
- The function f lies in the lower right region. It includes a point P at coordinates (x₀, f(x₀)) with a tangent line representing its slope at x₀.
- The inverse function g lies in the upper left region. It includes a corresponding point Q at coordinates (f(x₀), x₀) with a tangent line representing its slope at f(x₀).
- A dashed diagonal line passing through the origin represents y = x, illustrating the symmetry between the two curves and their points P and Q.

pg_171__page_66_Figure_6.jpeg.description: A graph illustrating the linear approximation (tangent line approximation) of a function y = f(x) at x = a. The Cartesian coordinate system shows positive x and y axes. A smooth, concave-down blue curve representing the function y = f(x) increases from left to right in the first quadrant. At x = a, a black point lies on the curve, with a vertical dashed line connecting x = a on the horizontal axis to this point. A straight black tangent line touches the blue curve at this point (a, f(a)), demonstrating how the tangent line stays very close to the function's curve near x = a.

pg_171__page_67_Figure_15.jpeg.description: A graph illustrating the geometric interpretation of differentials on a Cartesian coordinate plane with x and y axes.
